Front: What is a 'quality attribute' in software architecture?
Back: A non-functional property the system is measured on besides correctness: performance, scalability, availability, reliability, security, maintainability, evolvability, observability, cost-efficiency. The architect's first job is to RANK these for the system at hand — you cannot maximize all of them.

Front: What are the three types of constraints?
Back: Hard (regulatory, physical, contractual — non-negotiable), Soft (organizational, budgetary — flexible), Self-imposed (decisions you made earlier that feel like constraints but aren't). Naming each correctly is half the job.

Front: Name the canonical latency numbers every architect should know
Back: L1 cache: 0.5ns. RAM: 100ns. SSD random read: 150μs. Datacenter RTT: 0.5ms. Cross-continent RTT: 150ms. 1Gbps network: ~10μs/KB.

Front: What's the difference between SLI, SLO, and SLA?
Back: SLI = the metric (e.g., 'p99 request latency'). SLO = the internal target (e.g., 'p99 < 200ms'). SLA = the contract with consequences (e.g., 'breach = refund'). Rule: SLO < SLA always; the gap is your error budget.

Front: What is the error budget concept?
Back: Error budget = (1 - SLO) over a time window. E.g., 99.9% SLO over 30 days = 43 min downtime allowed. Burn rate determines whether you can ship risky changes. Once budget is gone, freeze risky work.

Front: What are Type 1 and Type 2 decisions (Bezos)?
Back: Type 1: one-way doors — hard or impossible to reverse (e.g., core data model, language choice). Spend time. Type 2: two-way doors — easy to undo (e.g., monitoring vendor, internal API). Move fast. Architects flip the common engineering bias: over-debate Type 2, under-debate Type 1.

Front: What's the 7-question decision framework?
Back: 1) What problem? 2) What constraints? 3) Rank quality attributes? 4) What options (>=2)? 5) Trade-offs of each? 6) Best fit, why? 7) Reversibility cost? If you can't answer all 7, you have a preference, not a decision.

Front: What is the Two Generals Problem?
Back: Two generals coordinating an attack through an unreliable messenger can never reach confirmed common knowledge of an attack time. Proof: each ack needs its own ack, recursing infinitely. Consequence: no protocol over unreliable channels guarantees both sides reach confirmed state. Idempotency isn't optional.

Front: What does the FLP impossibility result state?
Back: In an asynchronous distributed system with even one faulty node, no deterministic consensus algorithm guarantees termination. Real protocols (Raft, Paxos) work by using timeouts — accepting they may not terminate in adversarial cases.

Front: Why is 'CAP = pick 2 of 3' misleading?
Back: Partitions WILL happen — P isn't optional. The real choice: during a partition, pick A or C. When no partition, both. PACELC corrects this: if Partitioned A or C; Else L or C (latency vs consistency).

Front: What is PACELC?
Back: Extends CAP: if Partitioned, choose Availability or Consistency; Else (normal operation), choose Latency or Consistency. Even without partitions, you trade latency for consistency. DynamoDB is PA/EL; Spanner is PC/EC.

Front: Name the consistency models from strongest to weakest
Back: Linearizable (real-time order), Sequential (same order on all nodes), Causal (causal order preserved), Read-your-writes (see own writes), Monotonic reads (time only forward), Eventual (replicas eventually converge).

Front: What's the difference between Lamport timestamps and vector clocks?
Back: Lamport: single monotonic counter per node — captures causality but cannot detect concurrency. Vector clocks: per-node counters — can detect when two events are causally concurrent (neither happens-before).

Front: What are the three roles in Raft?
Back: Follower (passive, replicates leader's log), Candidate (trying to become leader during election), Leader (handles writes, replicates to followers). Election triggered when followers don't hear leader heartbeat.

Front: For N=5 replicas, what R and W give strong consistency?
Back: R + W > N. So R=3,W=3 (strong, tolerates 2 failures both reads and writes); R=4,W=2 (strong, asymmetric); R=1,W=5 (strong reads but writes fail on any failure).

Front: What is a CRDT?
Back: Conflict-free Replicated Data Type. A data structure that automatically merges concurrent updates without coordination. Examples: G-Counter (grow-only), PN-Counter, LWW-Register, OR-Set. Used in Riak, Yjs (collab editing), Redis Active-Active.

Front: Why is Two-Phase Commit (2PC) usually wrong in modern systems?
Back: Blocking: if coordinator crashes after prepare, participants wait forever. Slow: synchronous coordination across all participants. Doesn't compose with high-availability designs. Replaced by sagas + single-node transactions + eventual consistency.

Front: What is 'fail-slow' and why is it worse than fail-stop?
Back: A node that responds but slowly. Worse than fail-stop because: traditional health checks pass; latency propagates through callers; cascade is silent until everything is degraded. Most modern outages are fail-slow, not fail-stop.

Front: What is 'grey failure'?
Back: A node 'seems up' (passes health checks) but is broken in subtle ways — high error rate on certain paths, partial data corruption, intermittent timeouts. Hardest failure mode to monitor for. Most modern outages live here.

Front: What's a B-tree's write amplification?
Back: ~1× (in-place updates). Each write modifies one page. Trade-off: random I/O for writes. Good for read-heavy workloads with complex queries.

Front: What's an LSM-tree's typical write amplification?
Back: 10-30× over the data's lifetime, due to compaction rewriting SSTables. Writes themselves are fast (sequential append to memtable, sequential flush to SSTable). Compaction is the long-tail cost.

Front: When should you choose LSM (Cassandra/Scylla/RocksDB) over B-tree (PG/MySQL)?
Back: Write-heavy workloads, simple key-based access patterns, eventual consistency acceptable. LSM trades read predictability and write amplification for raw write throughput.

Front: What are the four sharding (partitioning) strategies?
Back: Range (each shard owns a key range — good range scans, hot-spot risk), Hash (uniform but kills range scans, hard to reshard), Consistent hash (resharding moves ~1/N keys), Directory/lookup (metadata service maps keys — max flexibility, SPOF risk).

Front: What problem does consistent hashing solve?
Back: Naive hash sharding requires moving most data when adding/removing nodes (N changes). Consistent hashing on a ring moves only ~1/N keys. Virtual nodes (100-200 per real node) provide balance.

Front: Why are isolation levels important?
Back: SQL isolation levels (Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Snapshot, Serializable) control which concurrent-transaction anomalies are possible. Snapshot Isolation does NOT prevent write skew — a common production bug. If correctness needs 'if X then Y', use SERIALIZABLE or explicit locking.

Front: What is 'write skew' and why does it bite?
Back: Two concurrent transactions each read X, both modify Y based on it, both commit — invariant on X violated. NOT prevented by snapshot isolation (each tx sees its own snapshot). Fixed by SERIALIZABLE or SELECT FOR UPDATE.

Front: What's CDC and why does it matter?
Back: Change Data Capture: stream every change from the DB's write-ahead log as events. Tools: Debezium, AWS DMS. Lets you keep search index, cache, warehouse in sync with OLTP without dual writes. Solves dual-write problem.

Front: What's the difference between OLTP and OLAP?
Back: OLTP: many small reads/writes, ms latency, row-oriented storage, many narrow indexes (PG, MySQL). OLAP: few large scans/aggregations, second-minute latency, column-oriented (Snowflake, ClickHouse, BigQuery, DuckDB). Columnar wins at analytics because aggregations only read needed columns.

Front: What's a typical PostgreSQL OLTP write throughput per node?
Back: ~1-10K writes/sec for typical workloads. Reads: ~10-50K reads/sec. Beyond that, scaling reads via replicas or sharding writes app-side.

Front: What's a typical Kafka broker's throughput?
Back: ~100K+ messages/sec on modest hardware. Cluster of 5+ brokers comfortably handles 1M+ msgs/sec. Partitions = parallelism ceiling.

Front: What's a typical Redis throughput?
Back: ~100K ops/sec per instance (in-memory). Latency: sub-ms. Caps: single-threaded for commands; cluster mode shards.

Front: What's the difference between a monolith and a modular monolith?
Back: Both deploy as one unit. Modular monolith enforces internal module boundaries: package-per-module, defined interfaces, no cross-module DB access. Captures 80% of microservices benefit at 20% of operational cost. Most underrated style of the past decade.

Front: When are microservices the right choice?
Back: Organizations with 50+ engineers, clear domain boundaries, mature DevOps, business that benefits from independent scaling and deployment. They solve organizational problems (team autonomy) more than technical ones. Below ~30 engineers, you usually don't have the org problem yet.

Front: What is Conway's Law and why does it matter for architecture?
Back: Organizations design systems that mirror their communication structure. Microservices work when teams are autonomous; they fail when teams still coordinate on every change. Architects must consider org shape, not just code.

Front: What's a 'distributed monolith'?
Back: A microservices system where services are technically separate deploys but tightly coupled in practice — synchronous chains, shared databases, deploy together. Has all the operational cost of microservices and none of the benefits. The dominant microservices failure mode.

Front: What does hexagonal architecture optimize for?
Back: Separation of domain logic from infrastructure. Domain depends on nothing external; external systems (HTTP, DB, queues) implement domain-defined interfaces. Wins: testable domain, replaceable infra, code that outlives framework choices.

Front: What's the difference between event notification and event-carried state transfer?
Back: Event notification: small event with just an ID/key — consumer fetches details via API (more coupling, less data). Event-carried state transfer: event contains all needed data — consumers self-sufficient (looser coupling, larger events, more schema coupling).

Front: What's the Strangler Fig pattern?
Back: Incremental migration approach: identify a slice of legacy functionality, build new system to handle it, route traffic to new, decommission old, repeat. Old and new coexist for months/years. Don't believe anyone who says they'll migrate in a quarter.

Front: What's an Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL)?
Back: A boundary/translation layer between your domain and an external/legacy system. Translates external model to your domain language; rest of your code never sees the external mess. Critical when integrating with legacy systems or vendor APIs.

Front: What's the dual-write problem?
Back: App writes to DB, then publishes to Kafka. Either can fail independently → divergence. Retries don't fix it (Two Generals problem). Even worse: app crash between DB commit and publish leaves DB ahead with no event published.

Front: What is the Transactional Outbox pattern?
Back: Write the event to an outbox table in the SAME database transaction as the business write. A separate relay polls the outbox and publishes to Kafka, then marks as published. Guarantees at-least-once delivery; consumers must be idempotent.

Front: Why is exactly-once delivery impossible across systems?
Back: Fundamental property of distributed systems. Two Generals problem applies — you can't guarantee both 'message received' and 'sender knows message received' in finite time over an unreliable network. The practical answer: at-least-once + idempotent consumers.

Front: Three techniques for making a consumer idempotent
Back: Natural idempotency (SET status='paid' vs INCREMENT counter), Idempotency keys (store (event_id, processed_at), skip duplicates), Conditional writes (UPDATE WHERE version=X, optimistic concurrency).

Front: What's the difference between saga choreography and orchestration?
Back: Choreography: no central coordinator; services listen for events and react. Each service knows its part. Best for 2-4 stable steps, loosely coupled but hard to trace. Orchestration: a central coordinator (state machine) drives the workflow. Easier to debug and evolve; tighter coupling. Best for 4+ steps or complex flows.

Front: Why does every saga step need a compensating action?
Back: Because any step can fail, requiring rollback of earlier steps. 'Send email' has no inverse — emails can't be unsent. Plan side effects without inverses for AFTER saga completes (use Saga Outcome Event), not mid-flight.

Front: What is event sourcing?
Back: Store every state change as an event; current state = fold over event history. Powerful for audit trails and temporal queries. Costs: mental model shift, schema evolution pain, snapshot mechanism needed at scale. Use for domains with regulatory/audit needs; CRUD is fine for everything else.

Front: What is CQRS?
Back: Command-Query Responsibility Segregation. Separate write model (normalized, transactional) from read model (denormalized, optimized for queries). Sync via events. Different schemas, sometimes different stores. Useful when read/write workloads diverge significantly. Does NOT require event sourcing.

Front: What's the difference between per-partition and global ordering in Kafka?
Back: Kafka guarantees order WITHIN a partition. Across partitions, no order guarantee. To get per-key ordering, use that key as the Kafka partition key. Cross-key ordering is impossible at scale.

Front: Why is the 'failure cascade' the dominant outage shape in microservices?
Back: One service slows down → callers' threads block waiting → caller runs out of threads → caller's callers fail → cascade. The failure spreads even to requests that don't need the slow service. Every reliability pattern is, at root, a way to prevent or contain cascade.

Front: What is 'blast radius' in architecture?
Back: The set of components/users affected when something fails. Architects design to minimize blast radius: multi-AZ deployment, cell-based architecture, per-service caches, bulkheads. Smaller blast radius = smaller outages.

Front: What is backpressure and why is it essential?
Back: Signal from a slow consumer to its producer: 'I can't keep up — slow down.' Without it: queues grow unbounded, memory exhaustion, cascade. With it: producers slow down, retry with backoff, or shed load. At every queue/buffer, ask: 'what happens when this fills up?'

Front: What are the rules for safe retries?
Back: 1) Only retry idempotent operations. 2) Exponential backoff (100ms, 200ms, 400ms). 3) Jitter (add randomness so retries don't synchronize). 4) Cap retries (2-3 attempts). 5) Don't retry 4xx. 6) Combine with circuit breaker.

Front: What is a retry storm?
Back: Downstream slows down → every caller retries 3× → downstream gets 3× more load → slows further → more retries → cascade. Brief outages become long ones. Prevented by exponential backoff + jitter + circuit breakers.

Front: What are the three states of a circuit breaker?
Back: Closed (normal, counting failures), Open (fail-fast without calling downstream, after threshold), Half-open (after cool-off, allow probe requests; success → closed, failure → open). Tuning: failure threshold, min request volume, cool-off duration.

Front: What is the bulkhead pattern?
Back: Separate resource pools (connection pools, thread pools, semaphores) per downstream dependency. One slow downstream exhausts its own pool; healthy downstreams unaffected. Named after ship compartments containing flooding.

Front: What are the four common rate-limiting algorithms?
Back: Token bucket (bucket of N tokens refilling at rate R, allows bursts), Leaky bucket (queue drained at rate R, smooths spikes), Fixed window (count per minute, simple but edge-spikes), Sliding window (smoothed fixed window).

Front: What is load shedding?
Back: Under saturation, deliberately drop low-priority requests to keep high-priority ones working. Requires clients to mark request priority. Examples: dropping analytics queries while serving user traffic, deferring background jobs at peak.

Front: What is request hedging?
Back: For p99-sensitive systems: when a request takes longer than p95, send a duplicate to another replica. Use whichever returns first. ~5% extra load for ~50% p99 reduction. Only safe for idempotent reads — don't hedge writes.

Front: Why must every service call have a timeout?
Back: Without timeout, calls can hang forever, exhausting caller's resources. Default Go HTTP client has no timeout — this is a bug waiting to happen. Use context.WithTimeout for cancellable, propagatable timeouts.

Front: What's a 'timeout budget'?
Back: If your SLO is p99 < 500ms and you make 3 downstream calls, their timeouts can't all be 500ms. Allocate: maybe 150ms each + 50ms slack. Think in budgets, not raw timeouts.

Front: What is chaos engineering?
Back: Intentionally injecting failures in production (or production-like) to verify the system degrades as designed. Levels: game days (scheduled, engineers respond), latency injection, failure injection (kill pods/AZs), continuous chaos (Chaos Monkey).

Front: What's the 5-phase framework for a 45-minute system design interview?
Back: 1) Requirements (5min, clarify functional + non-functional). 2) Estimates (5min, capacity numbers). 3) High-level (10min, boxes & arrows). 4) Deep-dive (15-20min, 2-3 components in detail). 5) Trade-offs & scale (5-10min, what breaks at 10×).

Front: For Twitter timeline, when do you use fan-out-on-write vs fan-out-on-read?
Back: Fan-out on write (push) for most users: O(followers) write, O(1) read. Fan-out on read (pull) for celebrities (>10K followers) to bound write fanout. Hybrid: at read time, merge pushed tweets + recent celebrity tweets pulled from tweet store.

Front: What's an inverted index?
Back: Term → list of documents containing that term (with positions, frequencies). Foundation of every search engine. Query 'distributed systems' intersects posting lists of 'distributed' and 'systems'. Sharded by document (not term) in real systems.

Front: What is multi-stage retrieval in search?
Back: Three stages: 1) Candidate generation (~thousands from inverted index, fast). 2) Light ranking (BM25, basic features). 3) Heavy ranking (neural model, many features). Trades compute against quality at each stage.

Front: For a real-time chat system, where does connection state live?
Back: A registry (often Redis) maps user → which gateway server holds their WebSocket. Sending: look up recipient's gateway, forward there, gateway pushes via WebSocket. Each gateway is a failure domain — recovery via reconnect.

Front: In a ride-sharing system, why is matching often done in batched 'dispatch ticks' instead of one-rider-at-a-time?
Back: Per-rider matching is reactive. Batched matching every 1-2 seconds allows: better optimization (e.g., assign nearest driver across many riders), fewer race conditions, smoother surge pricing. Trade-off: slight latency increase for much better global optimum.

Front: What's the idempotency key pattern in payments?
Back: Every payment request includes an Idempotency-Key header. Server stores (merchant_id, key) → result. Duplicates return cached result. Critical for: network retries, mobile spotty connections, intentional retries by integrators.

Front: What is double-entry bookkeeping in financial ledgers?
Back: Every transfer is a debit + credit, summing to zero. Balances are derived sums. Append-only, never UPDATE/DELETE. Naturally event-sourced. Required for: audit, regulatory compliance, recovery from corruption.

Front: What is reconciliation in payments?
Back: Daily process: pull settlement reports from acquirers, compare with internal ledger, investigate discrepancies (missing, mismatched, late). Without it: money bleeds slowly and you don't notice. Underrated as a design concern.

Front: What makes an ADR title good?
Back: Decision-shaped, active voice. 'Use PostgreSQL for OLTP storage' is good. 'PostgreSQL vs MySQL?' is bad (a question, not a decision). 'Database stuff' is worst (vague).

Front: When SHOULD you write an ADR?
Back: When a future engineer would benefit from knowing WHY this was decided. If they'd just say 'yeah makes sense, moving on' — skip it. Always ADR Type 1 (irreversible) decisions. Don't ADR variable names.

Front: What's the 4-level C4 diagram model?
Back: Level 1 Context (one box for your system + external actors). Level 2 Container (deployable units inside). Level 3 Component (modules inside one container). Level 4 Code (often skipped — code IS this level).

Front: What's the most important rule for diagrams?
Back: One level of abstraction per diagram. Don't mix containers and components. Label every box with what it IS (and language/runtime). Label every arrow with what it CARRIES (protocol/direction).

Front: How is RFC different from an ADR?
Back: ADR: one focused decision, 1-3 pages. RFC: a broader proposal (often involving multiple decisions, multiple teams, weeks of work), 5-15 pages, includes migration plan, risks, rollout. RFCs often spawn ADRs.

Front: What's the architect's job at its core?
Back: Make decisions visible (ADRs, diagrams), align stakeholders (translation across audiences), reduce decision fatigue (set defaults, encode patterns), predict the future (anticipate which decisions will hurt), model the standard (write the ADR you want others to write).

Front: What three sources of influence does an architect have (since they usually can't 'order')?
Back: Expertise (they know more), Track record (their past decisions worked), Clarity (their explanations make sense), Relationships (they're trusted), Frameworks (they help others decide better). Title alone doesn't grant influence.

Front: What's the 'Plateau Trap' for senior engineers?
Back: Staying great at building but never learning to shape building. Reward systems pay them to ship features; they keep shipping; they never make the architect leap. Force ratio toward 50/50 building/talking, even at some shipping cost.

Front: How should you delegate to different seniority levels?
Back: Junior: tell them WHAT to do. Senior: tell them WHY, let them choose how. Staff+: tell them WHETHER it's even worth doing, let them define the what.

Front: What's the framework for delivering bad news (e.g., 'your pet project is wrong')?
Back: 1) Start with shared values ('we both want X'). 2) Name the conflict ('proposal is in tension with X because Y'). 3) Bring data not opinion. 4) Offer alternatives. 5) Let them choose — don't dictate.

Front: How do you maintain influence over time without becoming 'ivory tower'?
Back: Stay in the code (20-40% of time). Build prototypes. Pair occasionally. Run code reviews. Pure-paper architects get stale and lose credibility. Always-coding architects don't have time for the rest. Find the balance.

Front: What's the disagreement framework — 'disagree without damaging'?
Back: Make it about the design, not the designer. ✗ 'This is bad because…'. ✓ 'I have concerns about how X is handled — what if we…'. Public disagreement on arguments only; save personal feedback for private. Save political capital for high-reversibility-cost decisions.

Front: Why are architectural decisions said to 'decay'?
Back: The world changes (scale grows, tech matures, business shifts). A decision correct in 2022 may be wrong in 2026. The Discord Cassandra→ScyllaDB migration is the canonical example. Architects revisit decisions on their review dates with data — not by gut.

Front: What makes an ADR get read vs ignored?
Back: Read: short (1-3 pages), title is decision, conclusion at top, skim-able with headers/bullets, written for someone who joined yesterday. Ignored: 12-page treatises, buried conclusion, all upside no downside, vague alternatives.

Front: What's the 'New Hire Test' for an ADR?
Back: Hand it to a senior engineer who joined yesterday. Can they: read it in 5 min? Explain the decision back in 2 min? Name one alternative and why rejected? If no to any — revise.

Front: What was the root cause of the Knight Capital incident (2012)?
Back: A 9-year-old debug feature flag, repurposed for a new feature, triggered on a server where deploy was incomplete. Old dead code path executed without limits. $440M loss in 45 min. Lesson: quality attributes you don't name (operability, blast radius) will kill you.

Front: What was the root cause of the GitHub October 2018 outage?
Back: 43-second network partition between US East/West caused MySQL Orchestrator to fail over to a stale replica. When network recovered, divergent histories couldn't be cleanly merged. 24 hours of manual reconciliation. Lesson: failover automation needs witness for true 'down' vs 'unreachable'.

Front: What was the root cause of Roblox's 73-hour outage (2021)?
Back: A streaming feature increased Consul write rate beyond what its Raft cluster could commit. Queue grew unbounded; positive feedback loop; cluster degraded but never recovered without expert intervention. Lesson: consensus systems have throughput ceilings; need backpressure.

Front: What was the root cause of the AWS S3 outage (Feb 2017)?
Back: An engineer ran a debug command with a typo, removing more capacity than intended. The S3 index subsystem went offline, taking down many AWS services and a huge swath of the internet. Recovery took ~4 hours (cold-start time never measured). Lesson: sharp tools cause sharp accidents.

Front: Why did Discord migrate from Cassandra to ScyllaDB (2022)?
Back: Cassandra ops became increasingly painful (GC pauses, hot partitions, operator load). After measurement, migrated to ScyllaDB: cluster 177→72 nodes, p99 latency 40ms→5ms. Lesson: architectural decisions decay; revisit on schedule with data.

Front: What's the most important principle for choosing between A and C in CAP?
Back: Pick C (refuse service during partition) for: money, identity, inventory. Pick A (serve possibly-stale data) for: counts, feeds, 'likes', presence. The default 'we'll be available' is usually wrong for critical business invariants.

Front: What are the three architect mindset shifts?
Back: 1) From solving problems to defining constraints (the right question is harder). 2) From functional-first to quality-attributes-first. 3) From code as the artifact to communication as the artifact. Internalize these; the rest follows.

Front: How long does it typically take to migrate from monolith to microservices?
Back: Multiple years, almost always longer than estimated. Don't believe anyone who says 'we'll migrate in a quarter.' Strangler fig pattern: incremental, old + new coexist for months/years. Plan accordingly.

Front: What's the difference between AP and CP under partition?
Back: AP (Cassandra, DynamoDB): always respond, possibly with stale data. Reads return; writes accepted; eventual consistency. CP (Spanner, etcd, Zookeeper): refuse service rather than serve stale or split-brain data. Lower availability during partition for stronger guarantees.

Front: What's the difference between Type 1 and Type 2 decisions in terms of effort?
Back: Type 1 (one-way doors): ADR, multiple stakeholders, prototype, sign-off. Type 2 (two-way doors): ship, iterate. Most engineering teams over-debate Type 2 and under-debate Type 1. Architects flip this.

Front: Why is 'fan-out on write' bad for celebrities (high-follower users)?
Back: Write cost is O(followers). A celebrity with 10M followers means 10M writes per tweet. Bursts cause hot keys. Solution: hybrid — fan-out-write below threshold (e.g., 10K), fan-out-read above. Merge at read time for followers of celebrities.

Front: What's the role of a 'dead letter queue' (DLQ)?
Back: Where events go after N failed retries by consumers. Out-of-band investigation/replay. Every consumer should have a DLQ. Without it: poison messages block progress indefinitely OR are silently dropped.

Front: What's a 'process manager' in event-driven architecture?
Back: A long-running stateful service that orchestrates a multi-step workflow across services. Listens for events, sends commands, tracks state machine. Distinct from domain logic — handles orchestration across boundaries. Sometimes called 'saga orchestrator'.

Front: What is the schema-evolution rule for event-driven systems?
Back: Events live forever. Schemas don't. Use schema registry (Confluent, AWS Glue) with versioning. Backward compat: new code reads old events. Forward compat: old code reads new events. Avoid: deleting fields, renaming, narrowing types. Prefer: adding optional fields.

Front: What's the difference between fan-out, broadcast, and multicast in messaging?
Back: Fan-out: one producer, multiple consumers (each consumer group gets a copy). Broadcast: every consumer gets every message. Multicast: producer sends once, network duplicates to subscribers. Kafka does fan-out via consumer groups.

Front: What three sources cause hot keys in distributed systems?
Back: 1) Skewed data (some entities are more popular). 2) Skewed access (some queries are more frequent). 3) Naming conventions (e.g., date-prefixed keys cluster). Mitigate: salt keys, route to multiple partitions, cache hot reads.

Front: What's 'eventual consistency' actually mean?
Back: If updates stop, all replicas eventually converge to the same state. Doesn't specify how long. Useful when: counts, feeds, 'likes'. Not useful when: bank balance, inventory.

Front: What is a thundering herd?
Back: Many clients simultaneously retry/reconnect at the same instant (e.g., after a brief outage, at periodic boundary like Monday 9am). Aggregate load spike exceeds normal capacity. Prevented by jitter, exponential backoff, gradual ramp.

Front: What's the difference between observability and monitoring?
Back: Monitoring: predefined metrics, dashboards, alerts on known failure modes. Observability: ability to debug NEW failure modes from collected data (logs + metrics + traces). Monitoring catches things you predicted; observability helps with things you didn't.

Front: What does 'capacity planning' actually entail at an architect level?
Back: 1) Measure current peak load. 2) Project growth (DAU, RPS, storage). 3) Identify dominant constraint (often: writes/sec, hot key, GC pause). 4) Verify headroom (50%+ typical). 5) Define re-architecture triggers (when current design breaks).

Front: What's a 'cell-based architecture'?
Back: Divide users/traffic into cells; each cell is a complete deployment. One cell failure ≠ all users affected. Used by AWS, Slack, others post-major-outages. Smaller blast radius at the cost of operational complexity.

Front: What are the 8 Fallacies of Distributed Computing (Peter Deutsch)?
Back: 1) Network is reliable. 2) Latency is zero. 3) Bandwidth is infinite. 4) Network is secure. 5) Topology doesn't change. 6) One administrator. 7) Transport cost is zero. 8) Network is homogeneous. Print these. Tape to monitor.

Front: What is a 'witness' or 'arbitrator' in distributed systems?
Back: A third node (typically in a separate failure domain) that votes on cluster decisions but doesn't store data. Used to break ties / prevent split-brain. Cheap to operate; high value for consensus. Example: MongoDB arbiter.

Front: What's a 'shadow read' or 'mirroring' in migrations?
Back: Send the read request to BOTH old and new system; compare results; serve from old. Lets you verify new system's correctness with real production load before flipping. Used in Discord's Cassandra→ScyllaDB migration.

Front: What's the difference between optimistic and pessimistic locking?
Back: Pessimistic: SELECT FOR UPDATE — lock rows during transaction. Safe but blocks concurrency. Optimistic: UPDATE WHERE version=X — check version on commit, retry on conflict. Better concurrency; requires app-level retry logic.

Front: How is pgvector different from a dedicated vector DB (Milvus, Pinecone)?
Back: pgvector: extension to PostgreSQL — keeps relational + vector in one DB, transactional consistency, simpler stack. Limits: slower past ~10M vectors. Dedicated: built for similarity search at massive scale, more index types (HNSW + IVF + PQ variations), higher cost.

Front: What's a 'micro-batch' indexing approach?
Back: Instead of indexing each event individually (high overhead per call), collect events for short window (50-500ms), batch-index together. Trade off: slight indexing latency for major throughput gain. Used in real-time search and analytics pipelines.

Front: What does HNSW do for vector search?
Back: Hierarchical Navigable Small World: graph-based approximate nearest neighbor algorithm. Logarithmic search time. Multiple layers of progressively dense graphs; greedy search from top to bottom. Used in pgvector, Milvus, OpenSearch, Faiss. Default ANN choice.

Front: What's the difference between strict, sequential, and causal consistency?
Back: Strict (linearizable): operations appear in real-time order, all replicas agree. Sequential: all replicas see same order (not necessarily real-time). Causal: if A causally precedes B, all replicas see A before B (concurrent ops can be in any order).

Front: Why is leader-based replication chosen for most DBs?
Back: Simpler reasoning: writes go through one node, ordering is automatic. Failover well-understood. Cost: leader is bottleneck for writes; failover causes brief unavailability. Used by: most SQL DBs, MongoDB, Kafka (per-partition).

Front: What's the 'split-brain' problem?
Back: Network partition causes two parts of a cluster to each elect a leader / accept writes. When partition heals, divergent state must be reconciled — often manually. Prevented by quorum-based consensus (need majority, so two halves can't both have majority).

Front: What's gossip protocol used for?
Back: Each node periodically tells a few random neighbors what it knows. Information spreads exponentially. Scales well, robust to failure, eventually consistent. Used for: cluster membership (Cassandra), service discovery (Consul), Redis Cluster topology.

Front: What is HLC (Hybrid Logical Clock)?
Back: Combines wall-clock time with logical counter. Provides causality (like Lamport) but with timestamps close to real wall-clock. Used by CockroachDB. Trade-off vs TrueTime: cheaper, no GPS/atomic clock; less tight bounds on uncertainty.

Front: What's the canonical writeup of the Outbox pattern?
Back: Gunnar Morling, 'Reliable Microservices Data Exchange With the Outbox Pattern' (Debezium blog, 2019). Original idea older but this is the modern reference. Includes patterns for managing the outbox table at scale.

Front: What's the difference between read-replica routing and CQRS?
Back: Read replica: same schema/model, just multiple read copies of primary; transparent to app. CQRS: explicitly different read model and write model, separate stores, sync via events. CQRS is heavier but allows different shapes; read replicas are lighter but don't.

Front: What's the architect's question about every queue/buffer?
Back: 'What happens when this fills up?' If the answer is 'it grows unbounded', there's no backpressure — that's a failure mode waiting to happen. Always have a cap and a behavior on cap (drop, reject, alert).

Front: What are the four levels of chaos engineering?
Back: 1) Game days (scheduled, engineers respond). 2) Latency injection (slow a downstream). 3) Failure injection (kill pods/services/AZs). 4) Continuous chaos (Chaos Monkey killing randomly daily). Each level requires increasing operational maturity.

Front: What's the operational difference between 99.9% and 99.99% SLO?
Back: 99.9% = 43min downtime/month. 99.99% = 4min/month. The 10× difference in downtime budget often requires 5-10× the engineering investment: multi-region, automated failover, hot standby, faster detection. Choose carefully.

Front: What's a common 'distributed monolith' anti-pattern?
Back: Services share a database (so they can't deploy independently). Synchronous chains (so a downstream failure cascades). Shared libraries with version coupling (so a library change requires all services to update). Tight semantic coupling (so changes ripple).

Front: What's an example of a Type 1 decision in a typical web product?
Back: Choice of primary database. Programming language. Authentication mechanism (OAuth vs session). Build vs buy on identity. Data model for core entity. URL structure. Public API contracts. These are years-to-reverse.

Front: What's an example of a Type 2 decision in a typical web product?
Back: Monitoring vendor. Logging format. Library upgrade. Internal API contract (between services you own). Specific algorithm in non-public code. Code style. These take hours-to-days to reverse.

Front: What does 'evolvability' mean as a quality attribute?
Back: How easily the architecture supports new use cases or replaces components. Measured by: coupling metrics, ease of adding a new feature, time to swap an infrastructure component. Often sacrificed for performance — and missed at design time.

Front: What's the trade-off between strong consistency and latency?
Back: Strong consistency in distributed systems requires coordination (consensus, replication acks). That coordination has a latency cost — typically multiple round-trips. Choosing strong consistency means accepting higher latency, especially across regions.

Front: What's the role of 'idempotency keys' in HTTP APIs?
Back: Client-generated unique key per logical operation (typically UUID). Server stores (key, result) for some retention. Duplicates return cached result. Critical for payment APIs and any retry-prone client (mobile, integrations).

Front: How is rate limiting different from load shedding?
Back: Rate limiting: pre-set caps per user/IP/key, regardless of system health. Protects against abuse + fairness. Load shedding: triggered by system saturation, drops low-priority requests dynamically. Protects against overload. Most systems need both.

Front: What's a 'hot standby' vs 'cold standby'?
Back: Hot standby: replica running, in sync, ready to take over immediately. Higher cost, faster failover. Cold standby: backup data, no running infrastructure; restore takes longer. Lower cost, slower recovery. Choice depends on RTO (Recovery Time Objective).

Front: What's the difference between RTO and RPO?
Back: RTO (Recovery Time Objective): how long can the system be down? Affects: hot vs cold standby. RPO (Recovery Point Objective): how much data can you lose? Affects: backup frequency, sync vs async replication. Both shape your recovery architecture.

Front: What's the role of canary deployments?
Back: Roll out new code to a small fraction (1-5%) of traffic, monitor metrics, expand if healthy. Limits blast radius of bad deploys. Requires: ability to split traffic, automatic rollback, comparable metrics on old vs new.

Front: What's a service mesh and when do you need one?
Back: Sidecar (Envoy) per service handling: mTLS, retry/timeout/circuit-break, observability (traces, metrics), traffic shifting (canaries). Tools: Istio, Linkerd. Worth it when: 20+ services, polyglot, mTLS required. Not worth it for <10 services.

Front: What does CSP (Communicating Sequential Processes) give you in Go?
Back: Channels + goroutines = built-in support for CSP-style concurrent programming. No shared mutable state required. Used heavily in Go's concurrency primitives. Different from actor model (Erlang) but solves similar problems.

Front: What's the role of an event broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ, etc.) in event-driven architecture?
Back: Decouples producers from consumers in time (consumer can be down when event published), identity (producer doesn't know consumers), and rate (consumer can be slower than producer). Provides durability and replay. Kafka adds: ordering per partition, retention.

Front: What's the difference between Pub/Sub and a queue?
Back: Queue: each message processed by one consumer (load balancing). Pub/Sub: each message broadcast to all subscribers (fan-out). Kafka: hybrid — consumer groups give queue-like behavior, multiple groups give Pub/Sub. RabbitMQ supports both depending on exchange type.

Front: What's the 'thundering herd' on cache miss?
Back: When a popular cache key expires, many clients simultaneously query the database to refresh. Aggregate load spikes. Mitigated by: locking/single-flight (only one fetches, others wait), randomized TTLs (avoid synchronized expiry), pre-warming.

Front: What does 'p99' actually measure?
Back: 99th percentile latency: 99% of requests are faster than this value. Tail latency. Important because: averages hide tail; tail is what users complain about; tail predicts capacity issues. Architects optimize p99, not average.

Front: Why doesn't 'average latency' matter for user experience?
Back: Users experience individual requests, not averages. A system with avg 50ms but p99 of 3s feels bad — the slow tail is what gets noticed and tweeted about. Always think in percentiles (p50, p95, p99) not averages.

Front: What's the rule of thumb for capacity headroom?
Back: Plan for 2-3× current peak as everyday capacity. Plan for 10× peak as the trigger for re-architecture. Plan for 100× peak as research, not engineering. These numbers vary by domain but the discipline of explicit thresholds is universal.

Front: What's the role of Service Level Indicators (SLIs) in error budgets?
Back: SLIs are the metrics; SLOs are the targets. Error budget = (1 - SLO) over time window. Burn rate determines if you can ship risky changes. Error budget exhaustion → freeze risky work and fix reliability instead. Used at Google SRE.

Front: What does 'idempotent' really mean (precise definition)?
Back: An operation is idempotent if applying it multiple times has the same effect as applying it once. SET status='paid' is idempotent. INCREMENT counter is NOT. Required property of any consumer that may receive duplicate events.

Front: What is 'compensating action' in saga terminology?
Back: An action that semantically undoes a previously committed action. E.g., the compensation for 'charge card' is 'refund card'. NOT the same as a database rollback (the original action already committed). The compensation creates a new committed action that offsets the first.

Front: What is the SAGA acronym actually about?
Back: Not actually an acronym — named after the 1987 academic paper 'Sagas' by Garcia-Molina & Salem, originally for long-running database transactions. Adopted into distributed systems vocabulary in 2010s. Refers to a sequence of local transactions with compensations.

Front: What's the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling?
Back: Vertical (scale up): bigger machines (more CPU, RAM). Simpler, has a ceiling. Horizontal (scale out): more machines. No ceiling, but requires distribution patterns (partitioning, replication). Architects usually scale vertically first, horizontally when ceiling is near.

Front: What's the role of CDNs in modern architecture?
Back: Cache static content (images, JS, CSS) at edge locations close to users. Reduce latency, offload origin servers, absorb DDoS. Modern CDNs (Cloudflare, Fastly) also do: edge compute, JWT validation, rate limiting at edge.

Front: What's BFF (Backend for Frontend)?
Back: A small backend per frontend (mobile, web, voice) that aggregates calls to downstream services, tailored to that frontend's needs (payload shape, batch patterns, security). Used by Netflix, SoundCloud, large consumer products.

Front: How is API Gateway different from BFF?
Back: API Gateway: single entry point, infrastructure concern — auth, rate limiting, routing. Often runtime-shared. BFF: per-frontend, application concern — aggregation, shape transformation, frontend-specific logic. Often per-team owned.

Front: What's the data-residency challenge in multi-region designs?
Back: Some data (PII, regulated) must remain in specific regions for compliance (GDPR, country-specific laws). Affects: where you put primaries, how cross-region replicas are scoped, what's allowed in caches. Often forces region-partitioned architecture even when not needed for performance.

Front: What's the trade-off between cache TTL and consistency?
Back: Longer TTL: better cache hit rate, less load, more stale data. Shorter TTL: fresher data, more cache misses, more load on origin. Pick based on: rate of data change, tolerance for staleness, cost of cache miss.

Front: What's a 'materialized view' in CQRS context?
Back: A precomputed query result, stored as if it were a table. Optimized for read. Sync'd from source via events. Different shape than write model (denormalized for query). Often the read side of CQRS.

Front: What are 'natural' vs 'synthetic' identifiers?
Back: Natural: derived from real-world property (email, ISBN, SSN). Synthetic: arbitrary (UUID, auto-increment ID). Architects prefer synthetic for primary keys: more stable, no PII in IDs, no semantic collisions. Use natural for unique constraints/lookups.

Front: What's the 'noisy neighbor' problem in multi-tenant systems?
Back: One tenant consumes disproportionate resources (CPU, IO, network), degrading others. Mitigations: rate limits per tenant, resource quotas, dedicated tiers, soft/hard limits. Universal in SaaS and multi-tenant infrastructure.

Front: What's the role of 'feature flags' in architecture?
Back: Decouple deploy from release. Code can be deployed but feature gated; controlled rollout (X% of users); kill switches for runaway features. Flag lifecycle is architecture: flags must be cleaned up, audited, typed. Knight Capital incident was flag mismanagement.

Front: What's the right approach to feature flag lifecycle?
Back: Add flag, gradually roll out, fully enable, then REMOVE the flag and the obsolete code path. Most teams skip the removal step — leading to Knight-Capital-style risks. Maintain a flag inventory; audit regularly.

Front: What does it mean for an architect to 'set defaults'?
Back: Establish patterns the team applies without re-deciding each time. E.g., 'Outbox for all cross-service events', 'context.WithTimeout on every external call'. Reduces decision fatigue, multiplies the architect's influence. Defaults are policy.

Front: What's the difference between 'best practice' and 'context-appropriate'?
Back: Best practice: works in some idealized context. Context-appropriate: works for THIS team, THIS scale, THIS business stage. The architect's job: translate from best practices to context-appropriate. 'They do it at Netflix' is not justification.

Front: Why do many microservices migrations fail?
Back: Common failures: 1) Splitting before fixing modular boundaries. 2) Not enough DevOps capacity. 3) Team not actually autonomous (still needs coordination). 4) Distributed monolith (shared DB or sync chains). 5) Underestimating timeline (months vs years). All architectural, not technical.

Front: What's the 'cone of influence' for a tech lead vs architect?
Back: Tech lead: deeply influences their team's decisions. Architect: shapes decisions across multiple teams + sets organizational patterns. Tech lead's influence is depth; architect's is breadth. Different roles, different leverage.

Front: What's 'speaking the language of the audience' in stakeholder communication?
Back: Engineers care about HOW. Tech leads care about IMPACT and RISK. Execs care about BUSINESS OUTCOMES and TRADE-OFFS. Same idea, three framings: 'replication lag is 800ms' / 'reads can be stale by ~1s' / 'customer transactions are accurate within ~1s'.

Front: What's the 'pre-wire' technique?
Back: Before any group meeting making a big decision, have 1:1 conversations with key stakeholders. Find resistance early. Adjust proposal before public review. By the time the group meets, the decision is mostly aligned. Surprise in meeting = pre-wiring failed.

Front: What's 'async-first' meeting discipline?
Back: Send the doc 48+ hours before the meeting. Reviewers add comments async. Meeting is for resolving disagreement, not walkthrough. If reviewers haven't read it, POSTPONE. Saves time, deeper engagement, better decisions.

Front: What's the difference between 'rolling deployment' and 'blue-green deployment'?
Back: Rolling: replace instances one (or a few) at a time. New + old coexist during deploy. Blue-Green: run two complete environments (Blue=current, Green=new); switch traffic when ready. Rolling is simpler; Blue-Green has faster rollback at cost of doubled infra during transition.

Front: What's an 'immutable infrastructure' approach?
Back: Don't modify servers in place; instead, replace them with new versions (e.g., container image, AMI). Eliminates configuration drift, makes rollback predictable. Standard in modern cloud-native architectures. Trade-off: longer deploy times but more reliable.

Front: What's the role of a 'control plane' vs 'data plane'?
Back: Data plane: handles actual user traffic, hot path. Control plane: manages configuration, deployment, scaling, monitoring. Separation: control plane outages shouldn't affect data plane (so users keep being served). Critical for high availability.

Front: How does sharding by tenant compare to sharding by entity?
Back: Sharding by tenant: all of one customer's data on one shard. Pros: query simplicity, blast radius per tenant. Cons: unbalanced shards (big tenant hot). Sharding by entity (e.g., user_id): better balance, harder cross-tenant aggregations. Most SaaS uses tenant-sharding for compliance + simplicity.

Front: What's a 'request hedging budget'?
Back: Cap on extra requests for hedging (e.g., max 5% of all requests). Without budget: hedging can double or triple load. With budget: amortize p99 improvement over modest extra cost. Used by Google, Cassandra, others.

Front: What's the formula for 'rate of decay' in architecture decisions?
Back: No formula, but useful heuristic: tech stack decisions have ~3-5 year half-life. Scale decisions: depends on growth, often 2-3 years. Patterns: 5-10 years. Process decisions: 1-2 years. The faster the moving part, the more often to revisit.

Front: What's 'shifting left' in reliability?
Back: Move reliability concerns earlier in the lifecycle: design (chaos by design) → development (failure tests in CI) → deployment (canaries) → operations (chaos engineering). Reduces cost of finding issues (cheapest at design, most expensive in prod).

Front: What does 'graceful degradation' look like in practice?
Back: Recommendation service down → show popular items instead. Real-time price feed broken → use cached price with 'price as of X' notice. Photo service slow → show default avatar. Architect's job: enumerate every dependency and pre-design the degraded version. Don't let it happen at 3am.

Front: What's the architectural impact of 'multi-cloud'?
Back: Run on multiple cloud providers for vendor risk reduction. Costs: 10-30% more infra, much harder ops, can't use cloud-specific managed services (which are usually the best parts). Most teams who say 'multi-cloud' actually mean 'we want to be able to move someday'. Usually overkill.

Front: What's the right reaction to 'we need to be cloud-agnostic'?
Back: Push back. Ask: do you actually plan to move? When? What's the cost of being able to move? Most cloud-agnostic strategies cost 30%+ in ongoing complexity while preserving an option rarely exercised. Often better to pick a cloud, use managed services, accept lock-in.

Front: What does it mean to 'maintain decisions reversibility'?
Back: Build software in ways that don't lock in choices irreversibly. E.g., hexagonal architecture (swap DB without changing domain), feature flags (turn off features without redeploy), strangler fig (incremental migration). Optionality has a cost — design for the reversibility you actually need.

Front: What's the typical career progression for an architect?
Back: Senior engineer (5-8yrs) → Staff/Tech Lead → Principal/Architect → Distinguished/Senior Principal → Fellow (very rare). Parallel: Solution Architect → Enterprise Architect (more org-facing). Each step requires building less, shaping more.

Front: How is a 'staff engineer' different from a 'tech lead'?
Back: Tech Lead: leads a team's technical decisions. Staff Engineer: leads a domain (multiple teams) or a difficult system. Staff often has cross-team influence without managing anyone. Will Larson's book is the canonical reference.

Front: What's the 'glue work' tax for senior engineers?
Back: Senior+ engineers do work that holds teams together: mentoring, code review, design reviews, planning. Often invisible in performance reviews. Architects do MORE of this. Worth tracking and surfacing — important for promotion.

Front: What's the difference between 'influence' and 'authority'?
Back: Authority: positional power to require action. Influence: persuasive power to inspire action. Architects rarely have authority over engineers from other teams. They lead through influence: expertise, track record, clarity. Title alone doesn't grant influence.

Front: What's the role of 'tech debt' in architecture decisions?
Back: Tech debt isn't always bad — sometimes a deliberate trade for speed. Architects: 1) Distinguish deliberate from accidental debt. 2) Track it. 3) Pay it down before it compounds. 4) Surface its business cost to stakeholders. Untracked debt is the silent killer.

Front: How do you measure 'maintainability' as a quality attribute?
Back: Proxies: time to onboard a new engineer to the codebase, lead time for changes (commit to prod), bug fix turnaround, test coverage, cyclomatic complexity, dependency count. Hard to measure directly; easier to measure adjacent. Worth tracking trends.

Front: What's an 'architecture fitness function' (Ford et al.)?
Back: An automated test that verifies an architectural property remains true (e.g., 'no service has direct DB access to another service's tables'). Encodes architecture in code. Often implemented as: import linters, dependency analysis, CI gates. From the 'Building Evolutionary Architectures' book.

Front: What's the 'C4 model' in one sentence?
Back: Visualize software architecture at four levels of abstraction: Context (system + actors), Container (deployable units), Component (modules in a container), Code (classes/functions). One level per diagram. Created by Simon Brown.

Front: What's the right number of levels for system documentation?
Back: Hierarchical: high-level overview (1-2 pages) for execs, mid-level (5-10 pages, C4 Container) for tech leads, deep-level (component docs, ADRs) for engineers. Audience-appropriate detail. The same doc can't serve all audiences.

Front: What's the trade-off in 'one repo vs many repos' (monorepo vs polyrepo)?
Back: Monorepo: easy cross-cutting changes, atomic commits, shared tooling, single CI. Hard: scale (huge), build perf, ownership clarity. Polyrepo: clean ownership, smaller builds. Hard: cross-cutting changes, dependency management. Both work at scale; pick by team size and change patterns.
